newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Guatemala ends war with jubilant celebrations.
newsitem.headline: Guatemala ends war with jubilant celebrations.

text.p: Guatemala's government and Marxist rebels signed a historic treaty on Sunday ending one of Latin America's longest-running guerrilla wars, and thousands of Guatemalans erupted into jubilant celebrations.

In a glittering ceremony in the courtyard of the National Palace, leaders of the four main factions of the rebels' Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unit (URNG) and President Alvaro Arzu signed the agreement that formally put an end to a 36-year conflict in which 140,000 people died.

Though many Guatemalans harboured doubts about the treaty's ability to transform the impoverished country, a mood of excitement swept the central plaza outside the palace as Arzu came out to declare, "The war is over," to a crowd of 35,000.

In a clandestine guerrilla camp in hills just 36 miles (58 km) south of the capital, about 100 guerrillas fired their AK-47 assault rifles into the air, emptying their magazine clips as they watched the signing on generator-powered television.

Such was the exuberance of URNG followers in the capital, publicly voicing support for the rebels for the first time in their lives, that Arzu had to tell them to shut up for a minute of silence to remember the 140,000 killed in the war.
Arzu stood shoulder to shoulder facing the crowd with veteran URNG commander Ricardo Ramirez de Leon.
The crowd in the plaza erupted with heartfelt applause when Arzu and Ramirez lit an eternal flame, aided by a girl in a wheelchair who lost her entire family in the war.

"This day of justifiable and genuine national celebration is the most transcendental and significant in the history of our country in the last 50 years," Ramirez de Leon -- who dropped his nom de guerre, Rolando Moran, for the ceremony -- said in a speech during the signing ceremony earlier inside the palace.

Addressing hundreds of international dignitaries in a sombre suit and thick glasses, the ailing rebel leader defended the rebels' decision decades ago to take up arms because of the collapse of democracy.
But his message, like that of chief government negotiator Gustavo Porras, was one of reconciliation and forgiveness in a country once torn apart by fratricide.
"We can and we must create a better country, and this is the opportunity. Peace will only be what we make it," Porras said.
The leaders of many Latin American countries, Spain and Sweden signed the treaty.

So did Boutros Boutros-Ghali, secretary-general of the United Nations, whose tenure started with the end of the war in neighbouring El Salvador in 1982 and ends on a similar note in Guatemala. He leaves office at midnight on Tuesday.
Receiving acclaim for brokering the peace negotiations, the U.N. leader urged the world not to turn its back on the impoverished country now that it had finished the war.

The treaty cuts by a third the size of the 43,000-strong army, which for almost 30 years up to 1986 ruled the country with an iron hand and was responsible for atrocities that gave Guatemala the worst human rights record in Latin America.
URNG fighters will also return to civilian life. Their numbers have shrunk to 1,700, but they still live under arms in remote mountain and jungle regions, observing a ceasefire.

The treaty also strengthens the rights of the majority Indian population, the main victim of the conflict. The Indians have suffered massacres, disappearances and a brutal racism that is still far from being eroded.
But to carry the treaty through, international financial backing estimated as high as $2.3 billion will be needed. Arzu's government has gone the rounds cap in hand for support.
"The international community must not turn its attention away, especially in the critical early stages of implementation," Boutros-Ghali, who leaves office at midnight on Tuesday, said.
